I love Eminem's song, "I'm Lovin' It", as heard on the McDonald's commercials.  Why isn't it on this CD, Em?  I was looking forward to hearing you incorporate some optimistic verses into your songs --something you've conspicuously avoided over the years.  Oh, but I can tell, brother Em, that you put those endearing raps about your kid on your albums to prove that you can be compassionate, and that you're not the hateful, disrespectful man that the media purports you to be...
But, come think of it, wouldn't any parent be compassionate about their child at such a young age?  What makes you so special after publicly --and proudly-- humiliating your mother, or our country in an incredibly ignorant tune on this CD?  Am I supposed to be led to believe that because you care for your child (apparently the only thing you genuinely care about, besides money), as any parent would, that you have a sincerely compassionate side to you?  Are you kidding me?
You've cleverly conned me again into buying another one your albums, Mr. Mathers; "I'm Lovin' It" is a great song, and boldly displays your musical and lyrical ingenuity, while also professing your love for the great flavor of McDonald's food, but that 'I'm compassionate when my child's concerned, and thus I possess a compassionate side' stuff, I ain't buyin, dawg.
Here's the skinny on the Em, folks, especially evidenced on "The Eminem Show": He's merely two dimensional, with two --and ONLY two-- sides, both occupying 50% of his feeble mind...  One side: money; the other side: adolescent whining and hatred.  Oh, and that stuff you hear about his child?  It's an attempt to save his butt media- and fan-wise, thus maintaining cash flow, and hence, falls on the 'money' side of his dimensionality.
(NOTE:  I'm not implying at all that Marshall Mathers does not love his child, because I am sure that he does dearly.  I am simply questioning his motives to include material about his child on this album.)

With Eminem claiming that he is presenting hip hop in its "most purest, most rawest", I have to wonder where that assumption comes from.
Ultimately hip-hop is about self-expression, which Eminem does as well as any other artist in rap.  Unfortunately, rap egoism and heroism are different.  Sure, Eminem can rap, and he can do it with a brilliant flair for meter, rhythm, and vocal intensity.  The problem?  He's just not saying anything.
Of course, that is a matter of debate.  The fact that Eminem expresses anger and rebellion and individuality is contradicted by blatant sexism and homophobia.  On this album, Eminem's ego once again takes center stage, only now it is no longer the torn and shattered self-image of The Marshall Mathers L.P. but rather the self-important statement of someone who actually believes everything good people say about him, and has major issues with those who don't believe in what he says.
It's not that I don't understand.  It's not that Eminem hasn't made some decent tracks.  It's just that behind the rhetoric and the sneer, there isn't much going on here.

Let me start by saying that every single track on this CD (all 19 of them) is outstanding! The music is not only catchy, it's addictive. Eminem's forte is the use of simple words to create hypnotic and oddly magical art. Obscene and derogatory terms are bitterly expressive and speak volumes of the Eminem's candor and risky courage to express himself. His words are unapologetically offensive but not for the sake of shocking audience. When you get pass the awesome music (I am serious, the music is extraordinary) and get to actually to listen to the lyrics, you will notice that his rated-R words are not used out of context, so to speak.

reviewText: I have nothing bad to say about Eminem. He certainly is one of (if not the) most talented lyricists and performers of all time, and has changed the face of stereotypical rap music forever. His most recent release, "The Eminem Show" is no different, although it showcases a much deeper maturity and understanding of his past and those who played major roles in it. Peppered with raunchy skits and references to the major headlines over the past few years, "The Eminem Show" does not disappoint fans, but rather shows them a different side of the controversial superstar. Every song, although displaying the good ol' Eminem that America has come to love (and hate), has a different message and feel to it. From retaliation (shown in songs such as "White America", and "When The Music Stops") to angry, dizzingly clever (such as "Til I Collapse) and playful (like "My Dad's Gone Crazy" and "Square Dance") this album gives you a sharp kick in the face with awesome lyrics and beats produced by the amazing Dr. Dre from start to finish. Although (as I stated before) it is more mature than any other of his CDs, it still has those select few songs you will be sure Tipper Gore will be tearing apart any day now. In a showcase of how little money he spends on mother's day, he rips his mom in the vicious and genius "Cleaning Out My Closet", and in "Drips", he and D12 bandmate Obie Trice rap about graphic sex and the consequences of which. My favorites on the record would include "Sing For The Moment" (an amazing adaptation of Aerosmith's "Dream On"), "When The Music Stops", "Business", and "Til I Collapse", although every song is pure gold. As I said in the beginning, I have nothing bad to say about Eminem, and this album gives me no excuse to. Bottom line: It's awesome.

The Eminem Show is a nice effort by Eminem for 2002.  This is a good album but not as good as the Marshall Mathers LP and Slim Shady LP respectively.  One thing it does do is show Eminem's maturity and growth as an artist.  On the first full track White America, Eminem comes to the realization that if he were black he would have only sold half.  This is very true because black artists such as Nas and Jay-Z who are more skilled than Em, have never come close to selling an unprecedented 11 million copies like the Marshall Mathers LP has.  Well on with the rest of the album.
Business is a pretty good track.  It's one of those not bad tracks but not horrible tracks.  I used to love Cleaning Out My Closet but got sick of it after hearing it hundreds of times on radio and tv.  It is a great track though.
Square Dance has a mediocre beat but has nice lyrics.  Em does well on this one.
Soldier is one of the best cuts on the album.  Em raps with a slick and fast tongue and the beat is sick.  I guarantee you'll love this track.
Out of the next three tracks: Say Goodbye to Hollywood, Drips, and Without Me, only Say Goodbye to Hollywood is good.  Drips is a horrible track for Obie, he raps better on mixtapes.  Without Me is the pop-like single for the album.  It reminds you of The Real Slim Shady and My Name Is.
The next full track, Sing For the Moment is the best track on the album.  Despite the fact that it is sampled from Aerosmith, Eminem spits some of the realest lyrics of the album on this song.  I can really feel him on this one.  He explains the meaning of the gangsta rap that many rappers today feel they have a need to spit.
The next track Superman was funny and amusing to me at first, but now it's annoying to me.  Eminem should leave the misogynist rapping to Ludacris because Luda does it better.
The rest of the album's tracks are about average and don't really stand out.  The exception being 'Till I Collapse.  'Till I Collapse is the 2nd best track on the album.  It has the hook master Nate Dogg on it.  On this song Eminem reveals a list of emcees in order who he says are better than him.
He says "Reggie, Jay-Z, Tupac, Biggie, Andre 3000 from Outkast, Jadakiss, Kurupt, Nas, and then himself".  The list is pretty accurate.  Though I would put Nas after Biggie and Em after Nas and Redman especially doesn't belong at the top of the list.  Jadakiss is good but in my opinion doesn't even belong in the top 10 of rap.
Overall the Eminem is a good album and if you have the extra money then you should buy it.  There are some tracks up here definitely worth the money.
summary: Good album but not classic (5 star)

The Eminem Show takes a bit of a departure from Eminem's previous work. The Slim Shady persona is gone from all but one track ("Without Me", which is enjoyable, in a guilty sort of fashion), and Eminem's raps are much darker, and deeper. However, though this is the album where people rave that Eminem bares his soul about his past and family, the far more interesting material on the disc comes when Eminem raps about his relationships with the media, and society in general. It's obvious that Eminem is no dummy, he knows just how he's perceived by media and society, and what's more, he basically admits that he's carefully cultivated this image (epsecially on "Without Me" where he raps about how no one wants Marshall anymore, but only the Slim Shady character). This investigation into the larger than life persona has created for himself provides a lot of really rewarding material on the disc.
Musically, the CD is well put together, for the most part. The Aerosmith sample on "Sing for the Moment" doesn't necessarily fit with the rest of the vibe for the CD, but for the most part the hooks are excellent, and well produced. Lyrically, Eminem is at the top of his game. Whaever streed credit he may or may not have, he continues to prove that he is an extremely talented MC who can hold his own in the rap arena.
This CD is definately the best of Eminem's mainstream releases, and is of interest to anyone who would like to get inside the mind of the world's most popular rapper trying to come to grips with who and what he is.

The Eminem Show is the first hip-hop or rap CD I ever bought & I like it a lot. Then there are the lyrics which, in my opinion, make this CD so great.
The Eminem Show reminds me a lot of Bob Dylan's early records. Stylistically, they are clearly very different.  But like Dylan, Eminem is very smart, and his intelligence is what makes him such a great lyricist (Eminem is more literal).  Also like the young Dylan, Eminem's favorite subject is the flawed human being, especially women who have hurt him, hypocrites and users in all forms.  He is emotionally raw, often sardonic, very angry and he is not afraid to mock and even show contempt for his fans (his white fans at least).  Moreover, Eminem can be mean - - but for all the flak he takes I don't think he is truly as mean as Dylan; he's just uses obscene language so it seems meaner.  (For example, Like A Rolling Stone oozes with a contempt and scorn for the people who listened to Dylan's music (the hippies) that Eminem has not matched.  And  Positively 4th Street must be the meanest song in the history of pop music.)

While both Slim Shady and Marshall Mathers are an important part of this CD, Eminem subsumes his two other personas to take center stage on The Eminem Show.  While the album is not as consistently impressive as either of his first two albums, it contains some standout tracks and displays a unity of purpose and theme that marks Eminem as a more mature and talented artist more than comfortable in his own often-criticized skin.  There is plenty of violence and cursing throughout the course of this exceedingly long release (coming in at over an hour and seventeen minutes), yet a softer and certainly more introspective Eminem sometimes reveals himself in the lyrics.  While there is plenty of talk about his own life, it is now somewhat counterbalanced by criticism of the music industry, censorship, and even American policy (including, as everyone probably knows, some harsh words for Lynn Cheney and Tipper Gore).  This doesn't make Eminem a global spokesman for anything, but it certainly seems he is trying to place his music in a larger context.  Naturally, though, his most intense lyrics revolve around his own life, the penultimate example of which is Cleaning Out My Closet.  In this self-revelatory track, Eminem launches a vicious attack on his mother, seemingly holding nothing back at all in his diatribe.  He raises the specter of his ex-wife Kim in The Kiss skit, but there is no equivalent track to Bonnie and Clyde 97 or Kim on this album.

Eminem doesn't take himself too seriously, leading to tracks such My Dad's Gone Crazy, the brilliant and funny duo with his daughter Hailie Jade.  Hailie's influence is felt most strongly, of course, on Hailey's Song.  This is by far my favorite song on this album, and it is certainly unique in that Eminem actually sings the lyrics, reflecting the obvious joy he feels at getting his daughter back.  There are certainly enough tracks reflecting the rage and youthful exasperation that have always driven Eminem, but there is also a measure of fun rarely felt in his earlier efforts.  Without Me is loads of fun, forever conjuring up images in my mind of Eminem in that superhero getup from the video.  In White America, Eminem seems to take delight in pondering the effects he has on young people; and I find a lot of entertainment values in Square Dance.  The only song I don't really care for is Drips featuring Obie Trice, a song that seems to take shock value for its own sake a little too far for my tastes.  Overall, though, The Eminem Show is yet another amazing album from the unstoppable force known as Eminem, and the maturity, commitment, and ever-increasing skills revealed in its conception and execution offer undeniable proof that hip hop's most controversial and influential star is going to be a force in the business for a very long time.

Eminem came into the game with a bang, and judging by this streak of quality work, he's gonna leave with one too. A few years ago, his debut LP, "The Slim Shady LP", showed us a party-happy and somewhat depressed Mathers. A year later, "The Marshall Mathers LP" hit us with the dark side of this man. And most recently, this "The Eminem Show" will have us viewing Eminem's revived and content state.
As with his past 2 CD's, this disc is quality all the way through. It starts off with "White America", a hard hitting serious track about the way the country is being lead. The flow and beat of this is slow and introduces us to Eminem's improved vocals. After this track, the CD follows with: "Business", Produced by Dr. Dre himself, "Squaredance", a diss to Canibus, and "Without Me", the album's first single and upbeat party theme. On track 12, Eminem shows us some old-school Mathers 'sounding flows with "Sing For The Moment", sampling Aerosmith's "Dream On" beat. The following tracks on the CD are all very good, with "Superman" (the 3rd single) and "Till I Collapse", a fierce song featuring Nate Dogg, probably at the top of the list.
Although I believe this CD ranks slightly below The Marshall Mathers LP, and just slightly above The Slim Shady LP, it's still a masterpiece. I've been an Eminem fan for a long time and even if not quite my favorite work of his, I can easily say these songs are the most professional and most clever cuts he has ever put out. No hip hop fan has a complete collection without this album in their rack!

reviewText:
Eminem has established himself as a household name, and probably the most well-known rap artist of his generation.  He has produced 3 multi-platinum CDs in 4 years and has released over a dozen singles.  His lyrics are amazing, and his production is nearly flawless.  His nasal flow has worked its way into nearly all of America's ears.  All of his CDs are non-fast-forward works of brilliant art, and this is no exception.  I love Eminem, and this is a great album from him.  I reccomend it to everyone, not just because of its brilliance, but also because it can be enjoyed but almost everyone as long as you don't mind cursing and some downright disgusting lyrics.
Here's my track-by-tracj analysis:
1. "Curtains Up" - It's just an intro, not as entertaining as the other 2.
2. "White America" (5/5) - An angry song with a cool video.  Great with good lyrics and a hard beat.  Gets tired after too many listens though.
3. "Business" (5/5) - Great song, upbeat fast paced beat and great lyrics.
4. "Cleanin Out My Closet" (5/5) - Heartfelt, good song.  Really enjoyed it.  Good video also.
5. "Square Dance" (4/5) - Upbeat, good lyrics.  Anti-Bush but whatever.  Took a few listens to get used to though.
6. "The Kiss" - Skit, not as good as others I've heard from Eminem.
7. "Soldier" (5/5) - Hard song, great.  Pretty good lyrics also.
8. "Say Goodbye To Hollywood" (5/5) - Great at first, gets a little annoying after awhile though.
9. "Drips" (4/5) - Annoying at first, but gets better after some listens.  Good although nasty lyrics.
10. "Without Me" (4/5) - Great upbeat song, funny and good lyrics.  Loses a point because it was overplayed.
11. "Paul Rosenberg" - Another below average skit.
12. "Sing For The Moment" (5/5) - Amazing song, phenomenal lyrics.  Great chorus by Aerosmith, "Dream On" is a great song.  Yet another single.
13. "Superman" (5/5) - Takes a few listens to get used to, but an upbeat song.  Good, I liked it.  Good video though, i saw the uncensored version on my 8 Mile DVD.
14. "Hailie's Song' (5/5) - Heartfelt, a little overplayed on the radio though.  I really liked it thought, good lyrics, although Eminem is not a very good singer.
15. "Steve Berman" - Eminem really didn't do a good job on the skits with this album, I liked the others from his older albums.
16. "When The Music Stops" (5/5) - Good song, great verse by Eminem.
17. "Say What You Say" (5/5) - Another great song, especcially lyric wise.
18. "Til I Collapse" (5/5) - Good song with a great Nate Dogg chorus.
19. "My Dad's Gone Crazy" (4/5) - Great lyrics, takes a little bit to get used to though.
20. "Curtains Close" - The outro, not good.
Overall, I felt that this was another phenomanal effort by Eminem, a great record.  A lot of hits too, "White America", "Cleanin Out My Closet", "Without Me", "Sing For The Moment", "Superman", "Hailie's Song", "My Dad's Gone Crazy", there might have been some more or less.

"Must follow rules. Must stick to content" (said in robotic voice).
OK, here's the high/lowlights of "The Eminem Show":
"White America"--Probably the most perceptive and aware track on the CD. Much like the comedy of Chris Rock: Vulgar but intelligent. Which is more than I could say for any other track.
"Cleanin' Out My Closet"--I should be paid for having to listen to this therapy session. Better to keep the closet door shut.
"Drips"--I'm sure young, immature junior high kids get a big kick out of this one. If there's anything nastier on the market than this track, I haven't heard it.
"Without Me"--Funny, I didn't think it felt so empty...
"Sing For the Moment"--Highlight of the CD. The Aerosmith backing track, that is, not the rap.
"Hallie's Song"--This is so tender and sensitive. But can't we do without the f-bombs on even this song?
"My Dad's Gone Crazy"--Mock scolding from Em's daughter. It goes past crazy to disgusting when explicit sexual references are used by "dad" in a rap featuring a daughter too young to be exposed to such vulgarity.
In total, an overly vulgar effort with not enough socially redeeming value to rate above one star. Has "poetry" come to this?

I've liked Eminem since the marshall mathers lp, but mostly just because he was [mad] and entertaining and i was [mad]. I didn't see much seriousness in it. This album is much different. Eminem HAS grown as an artist, lyricist, and a beatmaker (dre only did 3 songs here). He is no longer talking (entertaining) [stuff], he has something genuinely interesting and edgy (and sometimes profound) to say. HE is [mad], not trying to [make] the world [mad]. There's a couple of minor snags that ruin the album's overall flow, but regardless it's brilliant.
Track-by-track breakdown-
Curtains up: just an intro.
White America: Great song. Over an almost industrial beat, Em raps about the image he's created and how it's benefited him and at the same time made him look like a prankish [person]. In the intro and outro to the song he addresses the hypocrisy of this nation.
Business: Good fun song, great beat (even if it does sound a little too similar to the real slim shady)
Cleanin Out My Closet: Probably the record's most powerful song. This song is everywhere, so we all know what it's about. This is when em's at his best, when he's concentrated on one subject, and the impact of his rage is stunning.
Square Dance: More of em ranting on from topic to topic, but not bad at all. Funny canibus disses scattered throughout and at the end. Also some nice tidbits of political thought (not brilliant but politics are ignored in rap so this must be noted)
The Kiss: a skit with a dark, military beat at the end that segues into
Soldier: Another one of em's darker, angrier songs. About his issues with guns and also his dedication to rap.
Say Goodbye To Hollywood: Smart, sad insight into his legal troubles, but it contradicts the perserverance of "soldier" by saying that he wants to quit rap. Oh well, tupac contradicted himself too many times to be measured, and he's a legend.
Drips: I hate this song. Obie Trice [is bad] at rhyming and his verse is disgusting. Em's is better, has some interesting thoughts about promiscuity and std's. doesnt sound fake, but unnecessarily misogynistic.
Without Me: We all know this [darn] song. The only real Slim Shady song, mostly em stays in the real world.
Paul: dumb skit.
Sing For The Moment: Another rock-fueled song (samples aerosmith's dream on) about how em means something to his fans and that he cares about them. also a statement on rap and entertainment in general.
Superman: [bad] southern-rock beat, bad chorus, occasionally hilarious rhymes in the verses but nothing, even his intense hatred for kim justifies "put anthrax on a tampax and/slap you till you can't stand". He could've addressed his issues with her and other women a lot better.
Hailie's Song: Kinda sweet. Em tries to sing in the verses and chorus and although he ain't great, it's still full of love for his daughter. great rap in the 3rd verse.
Steve Berman: another dumb skit, but funny.
When The Music Stops: D-12 usually spends their time doing dumb hardcore posing, but on this song they all (even bizarre, his verse is hilarious) have a good point to make: rappers need to take responsibility for what they say and do. smart thoughts on the music industry. also a great almost gothic beat.
Say What You Say: Great beats and Jermaine Dupri disses courtesy of dr. dre and em. i hate jermaine dupri.
Til I Collapse: The best song. Spectacularly catchy arena-rock beat, utterly flawless flow brimming with energy and fury, and a good nate dogg hook.
My Dad's Gone Crazy: The last dre beat. Hilarious opening (hailie walking in on em [doing drugs]) and hailie in the chorus is cute. Verses funny at first, then kinda serious at the end. Another standout.
Curtains Close: You think em would resist the opportunity to bring back ken kaniff?

reviewText:
I first wrote a review of Eminem's "The Eminem Show" back at the end of 2002. When i wrote that review, i had only experienced listening to the album ALL the way through one time, so i didn't have the best perception of some of the tracks. Some that were my favorites then i don't like as much now, some that i hated then are really appealing now. My opions have changed for "The Eminem Show" and i now have an updated track-by-track review:
1. Curtains Up (Intro) - Just someone walking onto a stage and tapping a mic, probably Em. Didn't give it any stars.
2. White America (5/5) - I still like this track. The same angry verses from Em. I'm starting to get wore out of this one, though, but the video (which i could only find via the internet) is pretty cool looking.
3. Business (5/5) - Last time i gave it 3 out of 5, this time i gave it 5! Once i totally listened to it, i loved it. The music is upbeat and Em has a very catchy flow on it.
4. Cleaning Out My Closet (4/5) - I don't remember what i gave this last time but this time i'm tired of it. The radio (as well as MTV, BET, and other video channels) wore me out of this really fast. It has an OK beat but not my favorite.
5. Square Dance (4/5) - Whatever i gave it last time, this time i seemed to like it better. The beat grew on me, and Em's raps sounded somewhat better.
6. The Kiss (Skit) - Didn't give it any stars cause it's just a skit. However, it's a realistic portration of what happened the day of the 'kiss'. Blends in with the next song well, too.
7. Soldier (3/5) - I'm still not really feeling this one. The beat is alright, but Em's raps are too mediocre.
8. Say Goodbye Hollywood (2/5) - I just really don't like this one at all. The flow is WAY too long and boring and the hook is just not that good.
9. Drips (w/ Obie Trice) (5/5) - Last time i didn't like it that much, but after a few very careful listens, i love this track. Although Obie spits the nastiest verse i've ever heard from him or Em, Em does a pretty good verse.
10. Without Me (0/5) - STILL, i can't stand this ANNOYNING SONG. Follow my advice from last time Em: KEEP YOUR AIRPLAY TO A MINIMUM OR NEVER RELEASE ONE OF THESE [bad]POP SONGS AGAIN!
11. Paul Rosenburg (Skit) - No stars, just an answering machine skit from Paul Rosenburg, i never cared for any of the Paul skits anyway.
12. Sing For The Moment (5/5) - The latest single (how many singles will be released from this album??). Last time i didn't like it that much, that's only because i didn't hear it but one or two times, now, i love it. Em spits some very personal raps over Aerosmith's "Dream On" (i didn't even know what that song in the background was until i read a review saying it was the Aerosmith song).
13. Superman (5/5) (w/ Deena Ray) - Another single (the video's not shown on MTV, but you can see it one the "8 Mile" DVD as a bonus feature), this one i gave 3 stars last time, this time, i love it. Em's raps are really good and it's just an all around catchy song.
14. Haile's Song (4/5) - Don't like it as much this time (i heard it on the radio! I didn't know this was a single. There was no video or anything about it either so i don't know why they played it on the radio.) This is Em's tribute to his daughter, Hailie, who appears later on the album.
15. Steve Berman (Skit) - The newest installment of the Steve Berman skits. Their always the same, Em goes in, Steve says how awful the album is. But this time, Steve gets a suprise as Em brings his gun with him.
16. When The Music Stops (4/5) - Catchier than it was the first time around, now it's a little better.
17. Say What You Say (w/ Dr. Dre) (5/5) - Still my favorite on the album! Maybe "Drips" and "Busisness", maybe even "Sing For The Moment" all come really close, but i love this track. The nonstop beat and Em with Dre dissing Jermaine Dupri, what else could you ask for?
18. 'Till I Collapse (w/ Nate Dogg) (5/5) - Still love it! Why was this not a radio single? With Nate Dogg, wouldn't you think it'd be a huge radio success? The clapping is really addictive and Em spits some really good lyrics.
19. My Dad's Gone Crazy (w/ Hailie) (5/5) - Still a nice, hilarious, song. With his daughter, Hailie, singing the chorus while Em knocks out the rest, it's a perfect song.
20. Curtains Close (Outro) - Supposed to be the 3rd Ken Kaniff skit in the series but is only him on stage singing.
That's my new (and improved) review of the "Eminem Show". Other titles i recommend for fans of this album are: "Get Rich Or Die Tryin'" by 50 Cent, "8 Mile" (The Soundtrack) by Eminem and others, and the "Marshall Mathers" and "Slim Shady" LPS.
summary: My updated review of "The Eminem Show"

Marshall Mathers has certainly proved that he is more than just a white-boy-tryina-be-black rapper.  His lyrics are undeniably well-thought out, articulate, emotionally charged, and just plain genius.  He touches on topics that many rappers dare not come close to, such as his family and the depression that claws in the corners of his mind.  "The Eminem Show" offers us a window into the inner workings of Em's heart and soul.  The best thing about this album is that it truly IS Marshall Mathers--he doesn't act, he doesn't front, he doesn't try to conceal any aspect of his personality.  Just sit down and read the lyrics--there are underlying ideas and amazing observations in his songs that a person will never pick up on while listening to the record.  The words he writes with and his clever antics reveal that Mr. Mathers is a very intelligent, knowledgable man.  People who despise him because of his opinions or frequent use of profanity don't know him, and don't take the time to know him either.

reviewText:
I think Slim needs to feature more artists in his songs. 50 Cent, Xzibit, and more Dr. Dre would have been nice additions to the raps. Here are reviews for each of the songs:
White America - 9/10 - Nice raps, nice beats. Chorus is good too.
Business - 10/10 - This song is far better than "Without Me," and I don't see why it isn't a single.
Cleanin' Out My Closet - 8/10 - Very good rhymes, some were so ingenious that I was startled by them.
Square Dance - 9/10 - A comic song with a nice beat. Em's hillbilly voice is hilarious.
Soldier - 8/10 - Very fast rap. It'll take a few listens to get the words down. The chorus is mediocre, so you can listen to that easily.
Say Goodbye To Hollywood - 6/10 - Em messed up on this song, and the chorus is far too long. Worth listening to a few times, but not the best.
Drips - 10/10 - Very well done chorus. Obie Trice could have done some better raps...Nevertheless, his raps are nice and somewhat funny :) Slim has a nice, fast rap.
Without Me - 9/10 - You liked "The Real Slim Shady?" You'll love this one! The first single from the album that everyone heard months before the album even came out is one of the best on the CD.
Sing For The Moment - 8/10 - It's Slim rapping over Aerosmith's music. Nice rhymes and beat here.
Superman - 9/10 - Drips II.
Hailie's Song - 8/10 - Very catchy, nice to listen to.
When The Music Stops - 9/10 - No chorus, but D12 doesn't need one to be some of the best rappers around. Swifty McVay of D12 has the best part, Eminem just does a little catchy rap at the start.
Say What You Say - 12/10 - Definetly the best on the CD! A little reverse of what usually goes on when Dre and Marshall rap together. Dre goes slow and Marshall goes fast, and you'll find yourself rapping this song to yourself in public.
Till I Collapse - 9/10 - Simple beat, and Nate Dogg at his best. Em does some nice rapping, too.
My Dad's Gone Crazy - 10/10 - Comical and serious raps put together with Marshall's daughter Hailie Jade. A perfect combination! Fun to listen to. Has a nice, catchy beat too.
All in all, this is an excellent CD. I also recommend Man vs. Machine (Xzibit) and Get Rich or Die Tryin' (50 Cent) to go along with this CD.

On this album, the so-called "Detroit Demolisher" moves away from his trademark sound toward a musical style known as 'rap.'  It's an odd choice for someone like Em, but it often works.  What's really amazing though is the emotional openness of the album.  Eminem shows us the sad, terrified, crying little boy inside himself.  He is afraid of the world and wants to be protected, even loved for who he really is.  In this way, Em follows the sensibility of other "open-hearted" artists like Barbra Streisand and Liza Minnelli.

reviewText:
In the beginning there was The Slim Shady LP. This album introduced us to Eminems sick sense of humor. It was almost entirely fun and games. Then there was The Marshall Mathers LP. This was the same, but it added raw anger to the mix to make something that was only half-joking. Now we have The Eminem Show. This CD killed Slim Shady save a couple of tracks and mostly took the sick sense of humor out, and replaced it with other things. Pain, politics, and (who would've thought) love. He matured. This scared away a lot of fans, but Im glad he progressed.
One of my favorite things about this album is that its very diverse. There are two Slim Shady tracks (Without Me, My Dads Gone Crazy) to give the Shady fans something, at least. The first one is a mostly a diss track and youve all heard it. The second reminds us that even if hes gotten a little more normal, he still has his sick sense of humor and hes still a drug addict. Theres a couple political tracks(White America, Square Dance). The first one cusses out the government, plus it talks about how hes sold records because of his controversy and skin color. The second is partly about how tough he is, but its not really as focused. I don't know how I feel about these because I doubt Eminem knows very much about politics, but they make things more interesting. Theres some tracks about how theres been a lot of pain in his life and his fans(Cleanin' Out My Closet, Sayin' Goodbye to Hollywood, Sing for the Moment). The first tells you why he hates his mom so much and the second is about how fame is tough. These are pretty good, but not my favorites. The third one is. Its a different kind of thing because its about his fans' pain, not his. But I like it because its not just about him and I can sort of relate to it, even though theres not a lot to complain about in my life. Since its a cover of a rock song, it also ends with a really good guitar solo. Theres a few "Im so tough, so don't [mess]with me" tracks(Soldier, When the Music Stops,Say What You Say). Soldier is the angriest song on here, and gives me an anger release song that this album is usually lacking. The second is a D12 track thats better than almost anything on the D12 album. The third is a Dr. Dre track warning off anybody who would dare oppose Em or Dre. Theres a few mutant tracks that don't fit in any of the other categories. Business is an upbeat track about how Eminem is skilled and an essential part of rap. Good beat by Dr. Dre. Drips and Superman are both misogynist tracks, and I don't like either one. As Eminem continues to wrestle the media, his life, and his enemies, he puts it all on wax on "Show", a surreal look into his life. I remembered Eminem when his music was humorous. He was the equivalent of Redman, but not as good as Big L with the punchlines. After 2000's Marshall Mathers LP, Eminem couldn't go anywhere but down. But I was wrong. Eminem has flipped his own style and made a milestone record that shows great lengths of maturation. He's no longer stabbing gays, popping purple pills or smoking fat pounds of grass. This is the new Eminem we're most likely going to see for the next few years.
From semi-political (White America) to repetitive (Business & Without Me), the majority of the album is a darker Marshall Mathers. Here, he's saying something of resonance and thankfully his fans are still here waiting for him to say something that will piss people off. Well, he doesn't get anywhere near that level (maybe to Jermaine Dupri and Tipper Gore), but he joins Ja Rule in the Rapper Who Sings genre (Hallie's Song), but the only difference between him and that clown is that he says "I can't sing." The song comes off as touching and thankfully he raps on the third verse.
If you're a fan of Eminem, you'll notice he has easily slipped into his new style of rapping under the radar. But for the casual listener, they'll say, "Where's the homophobic references?" Now the question remains where can Eminem go after this album? He's already dissed Benzino rather well, but if he starts rapping about his movie experience, his albums will turn into the likes of Star Trek movies, or worse, Ja Rule albums.

However on this album has gotten much more personal, switched up the format and type or rapping on each song, created great hooks and finally beats that are just as predominant as him. So heres the breakdown of ths songs, skipping the skits:
White America: the pounding beats and Eminem's agressive tone match each other perfectly in this song with self-confessing lyrics about Eminem's rise that are not only shocking in what they say but because that Eminem is willing to admit them. From this song you know Eminem is much more focused on his rise to fame and the media's potray of him rather then jabs at his targeets.  8.5/10
Business-a good bouncy track with a great beat with eminem talking bout the rap game. 8.5/10
Cleaning out my Closet- one of the most personal tracks on the album about eminem's darkest issues, but mainly his mother. Rather than make jokes about her, the track is of grim seriousness and emotion. 8.5/10
Square Dance- this is a good song even though its got a strange chrous. A pretty good beat and some political raps. 8/10
Say Goodbye to Hollywood: another track with personal lyrics mixed with an desperationa and vunerability in eminem's voice. A good beat too. 8.5/10
Drips: this one of the lesser tracks on the album. Not really worthy of mention. An ok beat, but predicatable unorignal lyrics bout STDs and sex. 7/10
Without Me:the first single. Although its uncannily similar to his earlier first singles of the other albums. This is the albums most club-friendly song and has jumpy beat which suits eminem's upbeat raps. A good hook too. 8/10
Sing for the moment: An amazing song with lyrics about emimen's music, how music people affects people and plain thought-provoking. Grim music matches eminem's voice that is full of determination, emotion and edge. 9/10
Superman: although the lyrics are somewhat unoringal in comparison to the other one on the album. Eminem's flow on the song is a hook all itself and the chorous is great too. 8.5/10

The customer who buys The Eminem Show with sharp recollections of the vicious, sarcastic, inflammatory "Slim Shady" of the Marshall Mathers LP will be at once delighted, mesmerized and confounded by The Eminem Show. In that the songs offer onslaughts of epithets laced with all sorts of creative combinations of swear words and obcenities while exploring psychological caverns where civilized Americans don't want to go, The Eminem Show roughly approximates its vastly inferior predecessor. But with the exception of "Stan," the Marshall Mathers LP offers no glimpses of the expressive, ingenious snarls of metaphor, rhyme and alliteration that emerge, however infrequently, in the Eminem Show.
  The Marshall Mathers LP reveals an artist with a flare for rhyme, repetition and alliteration but whose verses consist mainly of piles of pedestrian cliches. Even in "Stan," a fine and varied rap ballad, Eminem resorts to lines like "you've got some issues" and "I think you need some counselling." Eminem struggles with this problem in The Eminem Show but to a much lesser extent. "Hallie's Song" repeatedly employs a reference to Atlas carrying the world on his shoulders: "sometimes it feels like the world's on my shoulders, / Everyone's leaning on me." But Eminem develops this conceit much further that he would have on the Marshall Mathers LP. No sooner has the speaker described himself  growing "colder the older" than he relates how the "boulder on his shoulder" grows "heavier and harder to hold," only to describe his "neck breaking" under the boulder's pressure. In conclusion he asks the listener whether he should "give up" or "live up to the expectations." The speaker's dread of losing his daughter is palpapable. The logic of the metaphor could not be more explicit.
  Eminem displays breathtaking literary skill in "My daddy's gone crazy." He uses his gifts for rhyme, alliteration and repition to produce a seamlessly connected sequence of images. The speaker transitions from posturing about his talent as a rapper to wailing in agony upon his uncle's grave in the space of a few lines. The speaker reveals how easy it is to "misinterept" his "tongue-in-cheek" lyrics. Eminem adroitly exploits "tongue-in-cheek" through the speaker's promise to "yank his teeth" and "slice his gums" before ever "biting his tongue." The verbs ("yank," "slice," "bite") are razor sharp and as a result the central conceit is vividly and sensuously conveyed. Eminem rhetorically situates the threat to "slice my gums" after "bite my tongue," which allows him to inifinitely extend his series of hypothetical propositions. The speaker promises to "get struck by lightning twice at once" and "die and come back as Vanilla's Ice's son." This conceits vanish for a few lines only to resurface, for transformed psychological insight and extraordinary emotional power, in the speaker's description of himself standing on "Ronnie's grave, screaming at the sky," while at the same time "clouds gather" ominously above the graveyard. Eminem uses the "lightning" to transition from the little girl "inside of a plane aimed at the world trade" to an ashen graveyard. The breadth of this journey across psychological and physical landscapes rivals Whitman in its breadth and heterogeneity.
  The logic of Eminem's lyrics falters at times. In "Hallie's Song" he asserts that the "years" he has "wasted" are "nothing to" the "tears" he has tasted." He means that the time he felt he wasted with Kim pales in comparison with the pain he felt throughout the tenure of their relationship.  "Years," a time span, and "tears," symptoms of grief, cannot be quantitatively compared. Eminem lacks the persistence to make this comparison fruitful. He needs to specify what he "wasted" during the years even if it means he has to search for another rhyme. The metaphor, as it stands, is meaningless.
summary: A relentless burst of meaning-packed metaphor

reviewText:
Fortunately for his fans, Eminem has not changed.  He still can rap, he still hates everybody, and he's still not afraid to say it.  Any doubts that he would be around for a long time are shattered once and for all in The Eminem Show.
However, perhaps realizing that pure shock value wasn't going to sell his records this time around, Eminem  added some more pop elements to appeal to more mainstream fans.  Several tracks feature him singing (poorly), and others show a sappy side of Eminem that doesn't really befit his style.  Most rap fans that I know don't buy Eminem albums for love songs and ballads about him cleaning out his closet.  Granted, on the majority of tracks Eminem shows that he hasn't lost his edge or his flair.  And mixing things up isn't necessarily a bad thing.  He just has to make sure  his original fans aren't alienated--which they aren't...yet.

Some may applaud his "creative expression"  and say that his experimentation with different kinds of music shows how he has grown as an artist. Yet it's interesting to note that the best tracks, like "Business" and "When the Music Stops", are where he collaborates with his old friends Dr. Dre and D-12, his backup group who still has yet to get the respect they deserve.  It may be like his old stuff, but that's what he's best at.  Afterall, since when is laying down phat beats with Dr. Dre a bad thing?
As he points out on the album, Eminem is our Elvis.  But remember even Elvis didn't write his own songs.  Eminem's an amazing talent as a rapper and and lyricist.  But he's not good enough to leave behind the people and the technique that got him to where he is now.  This album is very good, I just hope that his future ones are too.

Ok, everyone, it's about time that people put aside their doubts about Eminem's skills or staying power!  Slim Shady's third album, "The Eminem Show" proves once and for all that Mr. Mathers is extremely talented, in addition to being a lightning rod for controversy.  With his debut album in 1999, "The Slim Shady LP", it would easy to have written him off as another white rapper being a pretender to the throne of hip-hop greatness.  Even with catchy songs like "My Name is" and "Guilty Conscience" making loud noise on the Top-40 charts, critics were in a hurry to lump him with other 'Great White Hopes' that flamed out like Vanilla Ice (just a complete joke) and Snow (just never found an audience).  The success of his sophomore album, "The Marshall Mathers LP" shocked many and showed he had staying power, but the truth is, Eminem was destined for success from the start.

  First, Eminem is a gifted lyricist and free-stylist, which already separates him from the pre-fabricated hip-hop garbage like Ja Rule and such.  Second, he made the crucial decision early on to ally himself with arguably the most respected and skillful name in the hip-hop world, Dr. Dre.  With Dre's expert and ORIGINAL sound backing up Shady's vocals, it was inevitable that he would be successful and that eventually people would come around to realize his talent.

  "The Eminem Show" continues to show the evolution of that talent.  "Without Me" captures the same fast-paced, light-hearted slams at popular culture that "The Real Slim Shady" did on his previous album.  In addition to such 'amusing' songs like that and "White America", Eminem delves deeper into, and makes some peace with, his sordid past.  "Cleaning Out My Closet" goes right to the heart of his pain about his upbringing and his fractured relationship with his mother.  If his lyrics in this song are indeed and accurate depiction of his life growing up, then it's no wonder he's such an angry individual.  Yet, through that anger, he seems to be making peace with himself, even if it means terminating any relationship with his mother.  It's gritty, harsh, but real material.

  Eminem is branching out into movies now with a loosely autobiographical "8 Mile".  Early reviews there seem positive, too.  It's always fascinating to see what he will produce next.  The controversy he generates grabs people's attention the first time.  The skill and talent that he displays keeps people returning each additional time.
summary: Guess who's  back?  Shady's back!  With a vengeance!!

reviewText:
Eminem releases his third record with a vengeance.  This record is a great example of evolution of an artist.  I, by no stretch of the imagination, am a rap fan, but this album is infectious.  His music started as almost a novelty and has evolved into an amazing, remarkably clever body of work.  His records have improved almost exponentially.
"White America," an edgy, angry attack on all of those who attack free speech, is the opening music track, and it sets the mood for the album.  "Business" is a fun and lively shot at the record industry and the players in it.  "Cleanin Out My Closet" is an attempt to talk about his problems with his mother. (however many times she has sued him) . . .  I could go on and on, track for track, but all I would say is that this is the strongest work Eminem has released to date.  Dr. Dre shows up now and again on the album and never disappoints.  D12 shows up on a couple, and the ones they do, are better than most of the stuff on their own release. And of course, Nate Dogg, makes his staple appearance.  But, he does show up on the best song on the album.
Eminem grows up a lot on this record.  He moves away from the utter vulgarity that made his name.  (not to say that this record isn't vulgar).  He gets political.  He makes reference to current events. . He shows that he is the premier act on the market.  An A+, Five Star, Two Thumbs Up, kind of record.

I never thought I'd like Eminem, but this CD changed my mind.  I love it!  The rhythm, the emotion behind the lyrics, even the lyrics themselves, complete with expletives, just blew me away. Eminem bares his soul in every song, and by doing so, creates a tour de force.
"Cleanin' Out My Closet" is one of the most heartbreaking songs I've ever listened to. You can hear Eminem's anguish in the line to his mother "I never meant to hurt you." "Halie's Song" is surprisingly tender, a great song that still has the artist's distinctive stamp. "White America" makes for biting social commentary, and the often-played "Without Me" is hilarious. Eminem has constructed a diverse CD that is never boring.  Buy it - you won't regret it.

In case you didn't notice, the Marshall Mathers LP was VERY different from the Slim Shady LP. SSLP was a comical album, with lots of joking around, funny stories, and huge exaggerations... the only serious song on it was Rock Bottom. The Marshall Mathers LP, while still having some comical tracks (Kill You, The Real Slim Shady, Criminal...), was a much more serious album (Stan, The Way I am...). This trend continues with Eminem's third commerical solo album, The Eminem Show. While many of the fans of the Slim Shady LP are disappointed, this makes for an extremely solid album... so solid in fact, that I would rate it in the top five rap albums of all time.
Many people have complained that there are no standout tracks on this album, like Stan from MMLP. This is because the overall quality of the album is so high, that the best songs ('Till I Collapse, Soldier, Cleanin' Out My Closet) don't stand out all that much. While 'Till I Collapse is the best song on the CD (and possibly one of the best rap songs ever created... I'm hardpressed to think of a better one), the number two spot could be shared by three different songs; Soldier, White America, and Cleanin' Out My Closet. Soldier is a fast, angry song, reminescent of 2pac's work. White America is a political song, with amazing flow and meaningful lyrics. Cleanin' Out My Closet is slow, well thought out, and painful to listen to because of how horrible some of the things he describes are.
Almost all of the rest of the songs on The Eminem Show are extremely high quality as well. Square Dance, Sayin' Goodbye To Hollywood, Superman, When The Music Stops, and My Dad's Gone Crazy are all amazing songs, all of which would be considered the best song on any above average rap CD.
Eminem also includes a few poppy songs (Without Me, Business) to keep him on MTV and keep the money rolling in. While not bad songs (some of the best stuff you'll see on MTV), they seem a little out of place on this CD... it's obvious he included them just to appeal to the mainstream crowd (nothing wrong with that... everyone needs money).
The only songs this CD could've lived without are Drips and Say What You Say. Drips, while sending a good message (don't have unsafe sex), garbles it with pointless vulgarity. The song would be better with more substance and less shock tactics (do we really need to hear feminine fluids compared with sour cream dip?). Also, Say What You Say seems thrown together at the last minute (both the beat and the lyrics), not living up to the extremely high quality of the rest of the album).
One last note: Hailie's Song. Eminem's singing debut. I've heard mixed responses on this one. I'll put it straight. While Eminem is not a horrible singer (he sings better than most men I know), he is DEFINITELY not professional level. If you are looking for pure listening value, the singing verses on this song will not satisfy... however, the EMOTIONAL value of this song is amazing. The fact that he would put a song where he sings (and, as he states in the song, knows that he can't do it very well) on a commercial album just for his daughter shows just how much love he has for her. Sometimes, the emotional value is enough to make it a great song. I personally love this song, and would put it in the top five songs on the album (which is saying a LOT on this album). However, because the song is so dependant on emotional value (which a lot of people don't recognize), I won't even put it on the list, because 90% of people will be angry about it's placement.
As I stated earlier, this CD is an amazingly solid CD (eleven out of the fifteen songs on it would be considered AT LEAST extremely good by an average, unbiased rap fan). Couple that with the fact that the very top songs on it are some of the best rap songs ever created, and you have one of the top five rap CDs of all time, and DEFINITELY the best since Biggie's death (I'm not saying that any of Biggie's CDs were the best, I'm just saying that the CDs that have come out since are of lower quality).

In case you didn't notice, the Marshall Mathers LP was VERY different from the Slim Shady LP.  SSLP was a comical album, with lots of joking around, funny stories, and huge exaggerations... the only serious song on it was Rock Bottom.  The Marshall Mathers LP, while still having some comical tracks (Kill You, The Real Slim Shady, Criminal...), was a much more serious album (Stan, The Way I am...).  This trend continues with Eminem's third commerical solo album, The Eminem Show.  While many of the fans of the Slim Shady LP are disappointed, this makes for an extremely solid album... so solid in fact, that I would rate it in the top five rap albums of all time.
Many people have complained that there are no standout tracks on this album, like Stan from MMLP.  This is because the overall quality of the album is so high, that the best songs ('Till I Collapse, Soldier, Cleanin' Out My Closet) don't stand out all that much.  While 'Till I Collapse is the best song on the CD (and possibly one of the best rap songs ever created... I'm hardpressed to think of a better one), the number two spot could be shared by three different songs; Soldier, White America, and Cleanin' Out My Closet.  Soldier is a fast, angry song, reminescent of 2pac's work.  White America is a political song, with amazing flow and meaningful lyrics.  Cleanin' Out My Closet is slow, well thought out, and painful to listen to because of how horrible some of the things he describes are.
Almost all of the rest of the songs on The Eminem Show are extremely high quality as well.  Square Dance, Sayin' Goodbye To Hollywood, Superman, When The Music Stops, and My Dad's Gone Crazy are all amazing songs, all of which would be considered the best song on any above average rap CD.
Eminem also includes a few poppy songs (Without Me, Business) to keep him on MTV and keep the money rolling in.  While not bad songs (some of the best stuff you'll see on MTV), they seem a little out of place on this CD... it's obvious he included them just to appeal to the mainstream crowd (nothing wrong with that... everyone needs money).
The only songs this CD could've lived without are Drips and Say What You Say.  Drips, while sending a good message (don't have unsafe sex), garbles it with pointless vulgarity.  The song would be better with more substance and less shock tactics (do we really need to hear feminine fluids compared with sour cream dip?).  Also, Say What You Say seems thrown together at the last minute (both the beat and the lyrics), not living up to the extremely high quality of the rest of the album).
One last note: Hailie's Song.  Eminem's singing debut.  I've heard mixed responses on this one.  I'll put it straight.  While Eminem is not a horrible singer (he sings better than most men I know), he is DEFINITELY not professional level.  If you are looking for pure listening value, the singing verses on this song will not satisfy... however, the EMOTIONAL value of this song is amazing.  The fact that he would put a song where he sings (and, as he states in the song, knows that he can't do it very well) on a commercial album just for his daughter shows just how much love he has for her.  Sometimes, the emotional value is enough to make it a great song.  I personally love this song, and would put it in the top five songs on the album (which is saying a LOT on this album).  However, because the song is so dependant on emotional value (which a lot of people don't recognize), I won't even put it on the list, because 90% of people will be angry about it's placement.
As I stated earlier, this CD is an amazingly solid CD (eleven out of the fifteen songs on it would be considered AT LEAST extremely good by an average, unbiased rap fan).  Couple that with the fact that the very top songs on it are some of the best rap songs ever created, and you have one of the top five rap CDs of all time, and DEFINITELY the best since Biggie's death (I'm not saying that any of Biggie's CDs were the best, I'm just saying that the CDs that have come out since are of lower quality).

... His "show" this time is all snarls, not cutting satire; Marshall Mathers is on the defensive now, and he's reeling from his mother ("Cleanin' Out My Closet"), the price of fame ("When the Music Stops"), and the politics of his skin color ("White America"). Other than "Without Me," which recycles the pop shots at the usual chart toppers and other white rappers, the only real target on the rapper's third album is himself -- the choices he's made ("Say Goodbye to Hollywood"), the relationships he's failed, the respect he still needs ("Say What U Say"). It's Em saying, "So you want to see what I'm really like?" -- whether his audience wants to see those demons or not.
On the tracks, Mathers is at the ol' crossroads. He and Dr. Dre are starting to repeat themselves on the likes of "Soldier," "The Business," and "The Drips," and The Eminem Show lacks the overwhelming, single-minded force that The Marshall Mathers LP had. The best moments feel unique, yet somehow isolated from one another: "Square Dance" calls out his competition over a wild collision of synth drones and banjo; "Till I Collapse" sounds like a surging military march meeting Queen's "We Will Rock You"; "Sing for the Moment" is the album's "Stan," a hip-hop power ballad reinvigorating Aerosmith's "Dream On."
Still, there's something particularly endearing about Eminem's meek singing -- yes, singing -- on "Hallie's Song"; his true feelings can't be hid with a dis or an expletive, and he sounds as real rhapsodizing his daughter as on any of his best rhymes skewing pop culture. He says he's happy here -- and you almost want to believe it.

One phrase you will probably never hear said concerning Eminem is, "Eh, he's okay."  ...  With "The Eminem Show," however, Eminem seems to have become aware of his pop stardom ... and come out with a somewhat toned-down and much more accessible work.
Oh, you'll still hear the profanity fly and the bitterness towards his now-ex-wife spout, but Eminem now turns his attention to his own stardom.  "White America" is a scathing anthem aimed at the disapproving parents of his suburban teenage audience, reminding them that "Erica loves my .../I go to 'TRL', look how many hugs I get" and he's aware that "if I were black/I woulda sold half."  The first single, the unbelievably hooky "Without Me," plays along this theme, with Eminem acknowledging that he's the pop music scapegoat of the moment but that we should just deal with it because music would be boring without his scandalous presence.  A mildly amusing moment comes during this song when Eminem blasts Moby as a "36-year-old baldy ..."--as if he is 18 instead of 29.  The three women in his life are dealt with in typical Eminem fashion--his mother is blasted in the almost wistful "Cleanin' Out My Closet;" his ex-wife Kim has a couple of tirades directed at her, namely "Superman," which is a slightly cleaned-up version of the scary "Kim" off "The Marshall Mathers LP;" his daughter Hailie gets her very own song ("Hailie's Song," natch) on which Eminem actually sings.  Well, he's reasonably in tune sixty percent of the time, anyway.  Hailie also pops up on the busy "My Dad's Gone Crazy," chirping the lead-in to the chorus.  One hopes that the intro to the song, in which Hailie walks in on Eminem snorting [narcotics], is fiction rather than fact, though, as Eminem is so fond of claiming most of his raps are.
If you've ever wondered why the heck Eminem is so popular, one listen to "The Eminem Show" will answer that for you very nicely.  Insanely catchy riffs and suprisingly evocative lyrics abound, and even if the only rap you ever listened to is Blondie's "Rapture," you won't go wrong picking this up.  Of course, you'll get strange looks when your late-thirties white female self pulls up in your SUV at the supermarket with Eminem blaring from the system, but it's never too late to have a happy adolescence! lbum.  9/10.

Eminem does it again! With little help from his mentor Dr. Dre, Marshall Mathers has dropped another bomb on the hip-hop community. Eminem pulls no punches on his third, and biggest solo album.
In typical Slim Shady fashion he expresses his "love" for the ladies on tracks like "Drips" and "Superman", and he also goes after new victims in the music industry like Moby, Canibus, Mariah Carey, and Jermaine Dupri. But this album isn't about taking shots at pop-stars, he has songs that address our nation ("White America", "Square Dance") and hard-hitting rap songs for real hip-hop heads ("When The Music Stops", "Till I Collapse). The stand out tracks on the album are "Cleanin Out My Closet", "My Dad's Gone Crazy", and "Hailie's Song". "Cleanin Out My Closest" not only expresses Marshall's ill feelings towards his mother, but gives a closer look at why. "My Dad's Gone Crazy" displays Eminem's twisted sense of humor with his daughter Hailie providing vocals and "Hailie's Song", the highlight of the album, finds Slim singing about the love he has for his child.
It may be a long time before the hip-hop community gives Eminem the respect that he deserves, but he has definitely dropped another 5 star classic.

reviewText:
Let me just start by saying that I am intelligent enough to know that Eminem isn't a genius, but open-minded enough to not consider him a no-talent shock artist.  Eminem does have some artistic integrity and he has some market savvy too.  So the following review is written by someone who has heard enough music, (hip hop in particular) to not be easily impressed, but not so jaded or reactionary against what is new and popular that I want to pan the album just for the sake of being contrary.
The Eminem Show.  Its supposed to be a concept album inspired by the 'reality-based' entertainment culture of recent years.  The title is inspired by the Jim Carrey film 'The Truman Show' in which a man discovers that the  day to day events of his life are being mareketed as entertainment to the masses.  After two wildly popular albums Eminem finds himself under the spotlight, but instead of shrinking or inventing a persona bigger than he is...Eminem has decided to flash the crowd.  Look at me he says...look at yourself too he implies.  But before things get too uncomfortable or too preachy Eminem plies us with his intoxicating wit and verbal dexterity.
This is Eminem's most balanced, and most mature work to date. And its a good thing too, because we aren't so impressed with his tongue twisting polysyllabic rhymes anymore that it all sounds clever.  Just like all hip hoppers the voice and the delivery only stay hot for a little while (Ja Rule take note) and so there better be some innovation or substance down the line.  Em keeps it fresh by turning inward and being a little more human instead of the two dimensional rebel without a cause of the past. This time out, Eminem rarely promotes his drug use as a badge of honor.  Maybe he was little more sober in producing this album because it just doesn't have nearly as many boring tracks as his previous albums have had.  Its hard to make a CD that clocks in at 70 minutes engaging throughout, but Em pulls it off for the first time.  Sure there are some moments where he re-hashes old material (Drips and Superman come to mind) but the music is still engaging and Eminem's witticism keeps things interesting enough that you are going to at least pay attention, plus no one wants to watch him pick his sores the whole time so Em steps in with some fun bangers that are more traditional 'battle-rap-I-am-the-greatest' products (see Till I Collapse and Say What You Say).
Speaking of the music, its startling that Em has almost completely abandoned the production help of mentor Dr. Dre (who only contributes three tracks on the whole album) and mans the ship alone primarily.  The result?  Well if you like Dre's signature production than he is sorely missed, but Em makes up for it with more musical diversity on his self-produced tracks.  Its also interesting to note that Eminem seems to find adequate tracks to express his emotional growth.  Em still has venom to spew but it seems to be hitting closer to home now.  He isn't stabbing ex-wives and disposing of bodies with infant daughter in tow anymore, but getting more into the hurt that has come from his relationship with his mom, with his fans, and with himself.  And for a change of pace.  Em actually sings a lullaby type song about his daughter on Haile's Song.  Although barely listenable, one has to give Eminem credit for being bold enough to do something that could be described as corny when he has attacked the rest of the world so vehemently for their sentimental subject matter.  Its all the more courageous because his daughter seems to be the only thing he cares about besides his music and telling the world you value something is always risky.  Exposing his daughter to the public eye (even featuring her on catchy My Dad's Gone Crazy) and even boasting he is a competent father are all cannon fodder for those who wait in the wings to attack Marshall.
Saying that this is Em's most mature work still does leave some things to be desired.  He is still sometimes offensive just for the sake of it making hamburgers out of everyone else's sacred cows.  With the exception of racial slurs, there really isn't anything Em seems shy about saying to get a rise out of people.  If you found him obnoxious in the past, he is still obnoxious now, but if it didn't bother you enough to dismiss the Slim Shady LP, or the Marshall Mathers LP, than you are in for  much greater treat this time around.
summary: A review from an older, yet open minded listener.

reviewText:
In his earlier days (all the way back in 1999), it was easy to dismiss Eminem and his Slim Shady alter-ego as over-the-top, convoluted attempts to be funny.  Detractors tended to focus on his anti-gay, anti-women lyrics (although they are not any different than most other hip-hip/rappers' words), and his proponents set their sights on Em's amazing rhyming ability and a sense of the harmonious, rhythmic flavor of hip-hip that escapes most high-paid artists.  On his first disc, The Slim Shady LP, Em ranted and raved at the world and made a lot of money for doing it.  On his second, The Marshall Mathers LP, Em dealt with fame and controversy, although his raving still came across more as funny than anything else (Elton John agreed to play with Eminem despite protests from GLADD because he "got the joke," according to the rapper).
Enter Em's third major studio album, The Eminem Show.  Despite the title and the initial single, "Without Me," The Em Show turns its focus away from Eminem somewhat in favor of tackling some enormous issues.  After the typical skit introduction - a series of real/fake speeches cobbled together from different awards shows where Em won something - Em raps right into White America, a heady, accusatory song that puts him directly at odds with his main detractors: white suburbanites whose experiences are much different than Em's own.  Forth on the CD is "Cleaning Out My Closet" (also used in the trailer for Em's upcoming film 8-Mile).  The song lives up to its name: he manages to exorcise the ghosts of his hateful attitude towards both his mother and his ex-wife, attributing some of his anger to a father that left before Em was a year old and a hypochondriac mother who projected her psychosomatic diseases onto Em.  He raps about venereal disease on "Drips" (an excellent argument for safer sex) and conformity in "Soldier" before returning to himself in "Without Me," before heading off into skitland later in the album.  Also notable are the semi-tender ballad "Hallie's Song" (he warns you beforehand that he can't sing), and "Superman," which has nothing to do with the comic hero and everything to do with unreasonable relationship expectations.
Perhaps its making too much of Eminem to say that his lyrics are inspired; one cannot deny, though, that his anger at his situation and the crummy things that have happened in his life simmers right beneath the surface of this album, more of a middle-finger to the world than to specific people, as his earlier efforts were.  Em risks inviting comparison to Rage Against the Machine (not that doing so would be a bad thing), and although his anger could use solid direction, it's clear that his heart is in the right place - just because crummy things happen doesn't mean they SHOULD, and sometimes the only way to stop these things from happening in the future (or to call attention to the fact that they are happening now) is to drag them out of dark little holes where society likes to stuff them, bring them out in the open, and make them as shocking as possible.  Pure schlock-shock, a la Marilyn Manson, is out of style, and Em wisely stayed away from that on The Eminem Show.  Instead, he has crafted a burning arrow of rage and leveled it straight at the heart of hypocritical America.
He may not be Gandhi, but Eminem is more of an activist than, say, Martha Stewart.  Rap is the language of the underprivileged, and Em reminds us that being poor does not equal being black, and even the poorest of the poor have souls that need saving.  It's almost sad that it took the musical equivalent of a speeding train to raise this kind of awareness.  Every time Em goes on TRL, listeners can finally laugh WITH him at the sheer stupidity and hypocrisy of it all.
Final Grade: A-

Marshall Mathers is the first pop-music genius of the 21st century.  Ever since "The Slim Shady LP", this exhibitionist with a heart of gold has been carving out his own artistic territory - a kaleidoscopic synthesis of music, poetry, suffering, bad potty training, bad relationships, and above all, theater.  In the context of the stage show - look at the cover:  MM on stage in front of a closed curtain; now you see him, now you don't - this album is an a report from the field, so to speak, of the evolving Slim Shady/Marshall Mathers/Eminem personna, which is, after all, the slippery subject of all the art (is it enough to call it music?). So if you're new, don't start here.
"The Eminem Show" is a public pause, an opportunity the artist has taken to contemplate, confess, and comment on life-to-date.  One of the things that makes this line so compelling is that he is one very, very smart boy, and so his confessions and comments are very, very interesting.
His intelligence allows him create, within the context of performance, the illusion of intimacy.  By "illusion," I don't mean he's dishonest.  On the contrary.  Masks make shy people bold. I believe him, whether it's about his industry, his mother, his lawsuits, or how crazy he is about his daughter.  But this is, as the title tells us, a show. The reason it works is that it is so clearly the product of an open heart.
One of the other most noteworthy things about the album is that it is more musically ambitious than the first two.  The tracks are still lyric-driven, but MM seems to be honing his own musical voice, and that means that his music is becoming distinguishable from the cookie-cutter gansta rap that has been, for him, merely a diving board.  This seems consistent with his first two albums, each of which was an innovation from everything that had come before it - whether in "rap" "pop" or whatever.

I honestly didn't want to buy this CD. My knee-jerk reaction was to not be like everyone else and condemn this CD. But I got over it, put my money down and gave The Eminem Show a chance. I can honestly say that I have no regrets. I own Eminem's other two albums, and although they are good albums, you get the sense that Eminem is still struggling to find his niche. The subject on matter on those CD's are a little uneven, having depressing tracks following the bouncy singles. With the Eminem Show, Marshall shows that he is not just a flash in the pan, a pop-star for rap fans or simply a shock rapper. Aside from a few humorous tracks, this CD is serious business. Eminem shows he has a serious side, and let's it all pour out through this CD. The main thing I love about this CD is it's variety. The first time I listened to it, I didn't know what to expect from track to track. The album starts off with the intense "White America" and never lets up until the humorous ending of "Curtains Close" which features the return of, you guessed it, Ken Kaniff. There are so many great songs to acknowlegde on this album. "Hailie's Song" was surprising. When I heard that he was going to actually sing on the album, I thought one of two things would happen: It would work and sound great, or it would be completely horrible and corny. Well, it works, and it works well. "Sing For The Moment" is definetly my favorite song on here. Most people will notice it samples Aerosmith's "Dream On." It's one of the softer songs, but more powerful than anything else on the album. It also has a slew of great lines (They say music can alter moods and talk to you/But can it load a gun for you and cock it too?). Other noteworthy tracks include "Cleaning Out My Closet," "Superman," "Business," "Square Dance," and "My Dad's Gone Crazy," where Eminem doesn't miss the opportunity to poke fun at R. Kelly. Overall, this is an extremely well done and surprisingly great album. I suggest that even if you didn't like Eminem before that you give this album a chance. Look past "Without Me" and you will find this CD will have many rotations in your CD player.

"Drips" is a bizarre song of the same women-dissing genre, in which we learn that Obie did not use protection, facilitating the spread of infection carried by Denise, who is em's girlfriend, according to the song. Obie does a good job rapping. The guy has talent.
"Without Me" has been played so much that it is even unnecessary for me to say much about it. Em has the satisfaction of telling people off, and calling Mobie a [name].
"White America" is a pretty decent effort at feigning humility. What he says in so many words is that he is a superstar because of his race. But in reality, he is a superstar because he can rap. People are not curious about him because he is a white rapper, they are curious about him because he is a gifted rapper.
At the end of the album, on the track "My Dad Gone Crazy," em drops the act and plainly calls himself a "genius." He also says that when he speaks, it's tounge-in-cheek, so it's easy to misinterpret his verses at first. This progression of thought makes me dizzy. Are we to assume that he always speaks tounge-in-cheek? Is he ever serious?
Finally, I was not that crazy about em's allusions to 9-11. Here I have in mind the track "My Dad Gone Crazy." Either he does not understand the seriousness of what took place, or I simply take 9-11 too hard, because I could not help but find his irreverent references revolting. He is way too smart and sensitive to use 9-11 this way, and I believe this was not the most apt use of a significant event in world politics--a subject about which em knows little.
Overall, I obviously recommend this record. Em is one of the most talented rappers today, and he and Dre make a good team. If you are an adult, then you should listen to the uncensored version of this album. So if you want Shady, this is what this album gives you: a little  bit of irreverence mixed with some hard lyrics.
summary: A Genius or One of Your Kids?

reviewText:
I wasn't a big fan of Eminem's first two albums except for a few songs. When this came out, I heard two songs off it and they were awesome to me. So then I ordered this CD right here off Amazon.com. I just got it in today and the raps immediately blew me away and I had to take several breaks to recuperate. I must admit now that I think Em is truly talented. He literally wears his heart on his sleeve and spews out all the thoughts on his mind and mixes his words together to form clever rhythms. Here is my song-by-song review now:
Curtains Up - This isn't a song really. It's just an opening skit with sounds of Em making his way to the microphone. It was cool how he ended this skit by taking a deep breath and then my player immediately went to Track 2 when he screamed "America!"
White America - Slow rapping is included in this song so the fans of Eminem can clearly understand the message he is delivering here. Very catchy
Business - Not one of my favorites but I like the chorus
Cleanin Out My Closet - The title actually means that Em is cleaning out his mind of all the thoughts that need to be expressed in the form of words
Square Dance - Em's hillbilly voice in the chorus is a little annoying but the music is very cool and so is the rapping
The Kiss - This is a skit that actually has background music in it that leads up to "Soldier."
Soldier - The rapping is quicker than most of his other songs and there is a lot of cussing so protect your kids from this one. Better yet, protect your kids from the whole album. :) LOL
Say Goodbye Hollywood - If you exclude all the skits on this album, this is probably my least favorite song. It's pretty average and the chorus isn't catchy enough but it doesn't decrease the final score at all
Drips - Never got a chance to hear this one because it was removed from the album when they were editing it. Actually it's still on here but it's just three seconds of no audio and then Track 10 comes on
Without Me - This is the famous single you've heard so much about. I've heard it a million times but it's still pretty good. Unfortunately, it gets overplayed on the radio and it can get on your nerves after hearing it too much so, once you've had your fair share of listens, try not to listen to it more because you might dislike it then.
Paul Rosenberg - I feel some of these skits are unnecessary. Paul just leaves Marshall a message, telling him not to carry his gun away from his home.
Sing For The Moment - Eminem borrowed this music from Aerosmith's classic song "Dream On." He even had them featured in the song and they sang the chorus while he included his rap verses.
Superman - A pretty good song but it gets on your nerves as the conversation between Em and Dina Rea gets played too much.
Hailie's Song - Em shows how much love he has for his daughter and how much he hates his mother.
Steve Berman - Another dumb skit that's just on the CD to take up space
When The Music Stops - The music in the background really gets you moving. There is no chorus. Just nonstop rapping with five rappers featured, excluding Em.
Say What You Say - Good song. Nuff said.
Till I Collapse - Nate Dogg makes the chorus catchy and the rapping is normal and still good
My Dad's Gone Crazy - Hailie's voice gets very annoying in this song, but Em's rapping takes your mind off of her
Curtains Close - A skit that makes you cry because it's all over until the next album
summary: Very unique rapper with an amazing album

#2 White America- 8/10- I love the verses of this song and the chorus is good too, but maybe he could've been a bit quieter on the volume.
#3 Business- 10/10- This song is outstanding, and the "H*ll Yeah!" parts by Dr. Dre are amazing as well. I also like the background tune for the chorus.
#4 Cleanin' Out My Closet- 10/10- Although he's pretty mean to his mother at some points of this song, he probably doesn't mean it. But anyway, he actually can sing in this song. I also LOVE the background tune throughout the whole song.
